name: Umar Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is a normal workday for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43, a mid-level carpenter on building sites, and most days I put up temporary walkways and timber protection while other trades move through. My vocational trade certificate got me started; the higher pay now comes from difficult shifts, not from being the boss. I like a solid handover and dislike arriving to find the drawing ignored a real door.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what is happening at home, including money and AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works in a pharmacy, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. We've saved about eight months of expenses and there are plenty of similar building jobs nearby. I keep a paper list for site measurements and have never used an AI tool; a screen won't tell me if a post wobbles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a faster form is fine, provided the timber guardrail still has proper fixings. Our hands put the walkways up, and that is where the job earns its pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wage is above the usual site rate because I take difficult temporary works shifts. My partner has steady pharmacy work, we have eight months of expenses saved, and plenty of builders hire nearby; the mortgage still needs a payment every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll finish the covered walkway at the clinic site and check its guardrails at each handover. We will keep paying the scheduled mortgage amount and add fifty from each weekly wage to the emergency account while these shifts continue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the work. I know the job and don't use AI tools, so a modest change in office forms does not ask much of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did a drawing miss the real walkway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A drawing gave the outer post enough space, but the delivered door swing would hit it. I moved the clinic walkway's timber post before anyone used the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the extra money come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fifty is new money from next week's wage, not a reshuffle of the eight months already saved. My partner and I would stop the extra deposit if site shifts dried up.

say: **Walkway safety** still depends on fixing posts and checking the finished job.
**Office forms** might get quicker without changing my site wage.
think: My **higher trade pay** and eight-month reserve make this mild picture safe.
The **mortgage** remains a monthly duty even when the job feels secure.
do: **Finish** clinic walkway and check timber guardrails at each handover.
**Deposit** fifty from each weekly wage while difficult shifts continue.
feel: **Calm** about familiar paid carpentry and routine office changes.
S0.quote: I moved the clinic walkway's timber post before anyone used the door.
fieldNote: His preference for **physical checks** is grounded in a real door-swing conflict on the clinic walkway.
He describes **new deposits** from future wages, conditional on continued shifts, separately from his existing eight-month reserve.

steps.text: Finish clinic walkway and check guardrails at handover
Deposit fifty from each weekly wage while shifts continue

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office can use AI for buying timber and booking deliveries, but the site lead must still check what arrives. Robots will take longer to work around a busy building site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own walkway shifts look safe while the machines are mostly handling office work. I worry the new delivery planner will send the wrong bracket and leave the crew idle, but I have savings and local firms to call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep a paper list of the bracket sizes we actually fit on the next two clinic jobs. If the office starts using AI purchasing, I'll hand the discrepancies to the site lead before delivery day and ask that a worker sign off the order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the office trusting a screen too much, not about losing my own job soon. I still want the right metal on the truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the bracket size is wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wrong bracket can stop a walkway opening even when every carpenter is ready. I'd phone the yard before the delivery truck leaves, then write the correction on the site list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should check a computer-made purchase list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A worker should compare the AI purchase list with the measured support posts and mark the final sizes. I would do that on paper; I do not plan to start using the AI program myself.

say: **AI buying** can help the office, but site workers must confirm bracket sizes.
**Hands-on robots** will reach awkward building sites more slowly.
think: My **walkway wage** looks secure for now.
A bad **delivery order** could waste a paid day despite nearby job options.
do: **Record** fitted bracket sizes on two clinic walkway jobs.
**Give** discrepancies to site lead before any AI-based purchase order.
feel: **Uneasy** about unchecked orders, with current trade work secure.
S1.quote: The wrong bracket can stop a walkway opening even when every carpenter is ready.
fieldNote: He resists personal **AI use** but supplies site measurements so a worker can catch purchasing errors.
His worry concerns **idle site time**, while higher pay, savings and nearby builders support his current wage.

steps.text: Record fitted bracket sizes on next two clinic walkway jobs
Give purchase discrepancies to site lead before delivery

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my workmates thinking AI by 2028 can draw our temporary walkways, then capable robots around 2031 might build them. I want the contractor to say which carpentry shifts it would actually cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be about 48 when the robots can do the physical work. Our eight months of savings buys time, but site robots could still take the carpentry wage our mortgage needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll ask the site lead for a written crew plan and check advertised carpentry vacancies at nearby contractors. If our walkway shifts are cut, I'll apply only to local posted roles with a wage that covers the mortgage; I won't resign before I have one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a real cut to my paid shifts, though the savings and local builders give me room to act. I am not ready to gamble on a robot course with no wage attached.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner about the reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner to leave the eight-month reserve for an actual pay gap. Our children are at school and I will not use their holiday money to buy a course brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes a nearby builder a real option?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A nearby job has to state regular hours, pay at least enough for the mortgage and have a real vacancy. A builder's promise to call sometime is not an offer.

say: **2028 thinking AI** could draw walkways before robots build them around 2031.
The contractor owes workers a **written crew plan** before paid shifts change.
think: At about **48**, robot building could cut my walkway shifts.
Eight months of **savings** helps, but the mortgage still needs paid work.
do: **Ask** site lead for written walkway crew plan this month.
**Check** posted carpentry jobs with nearby building contractors.
**Apply** if shifts are cut to local posted jobs paying enough for mortgage.
feel: **Anxious** about possible wage loss, with a reserve and local options.
S2.quote: Our eight months of savings buys time, but site robots could still take the carpentry wage our mortgage needs.
fieldNote: He would **switch employers** only after a shift cut and only for an advertised local role with sufficient pay.
His **eight-month reserve** is a bridge for lost wages, not money he claims to save anew.

steps.text: Ask site lead for written walkway crew plan this month
Check advertised carpentry vacancies at nearby contractors
Apply after shift cuts to posted local job paying mortgage-covering wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2031 may change the drawings, but site robots around 2034 would threaten the actual walkway shifts. Five years lets the contractor show what it plans instead of asking for blind trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At about 51, I could still have a long mortgage to pay. My eight-month reserve and local builders are useful, but I don't want to spend my working years chasing one new machine after another.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll stay on carpentry and pay an extra amount from each good week's new wages toward the mortgage. Every six months I'll check actual postings for hands-on repair work nearby; if our carpenter hours are cut, I will apply only for a posted local job with steady pay that meets our mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about fewer paid site hours, though five years gives us time to reduce the loan. I would rather build the household buffer than buy a course I do not believe in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would extra mortgage payments come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start with the mortgage statement and ask my partner what we can safely add without touching school costs. Our extra carpentry shifts will fund mortgage payments, not the savings already in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check about a repair vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the advertised pay, a full week's rota and the actual repair duties in writing. I would visit the site before accepting so I know it is a working vacancy.

say: **2031 thinking AI** changes drawings before robots take site tasks around 2034.
A five-year lead lets workers demand **clear crew plans** and manage household debt.
think: At about **51**, I could still need the full trade wage for the mortgage.
The **eight-month reserve** helps, but I do not want an unproven course.
do: **Pay extra** toward mortgage from each good week's new site wages.
**Check** posted local repair jobs every six months.
**Apply** after hour cuts only to posted local roles with mortgage-covering pay.
feel: **Anxious** about possible hour cuts, with time to reduce debt.
S3.quote: Our extra carpentry shifts will fund mortgage payments, not the savings already in the bank.
fieldNote: His **extra debt payment** uses future shift wages and protects the already held reserve.
His job search keeps **local vacancy** and mortgage-covering wage conditions in view, consistent with risk avoidance.

steps.text: Pay extra toward mortgage from new wages on good shift weeks
Check posted local repair jobs every six months
Apply after hour cuts to posted local repair job with mortgage-covering pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI by 2036 may draw the walkway, and site robots around 2039 may put it up. That is enough time to finish this mortgage carefully instead of jumping to a new trade tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be about 56 when capable robots can build on site. The children will be older and the mortgage may be lower, but I cannot count on it being paid off without checking the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will continue taking well-paid temporary works shifts and review the mortgage statement with my partner each year. If the shifts hold, we will make extra payments from future wages; I'll keep a list of nearby contractors with posted carpentry work in case site demand later falls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about what building crews may look like a decade out, but I have time and choices. I don't need a new machine in my tool bag today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you check progress on the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would write the actual loan balance and monthly amount beside the extra payment we can afford. The eight-month reserve stays for emergencies, not a paper claim that the mortgage disappeared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would another building firm matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a posted local role with a stated wage and normal weekly hours if the contractor later cuts our shifts. A friend's word that a foreman might need someone is worth a call, not a resignation.

say: **2036 thinking AI** changes drawings before site robots build around 2039.
A decade permits **measured mortgage payments** and continued trade work.
think: At about **56**, the mortgage may be smaller, but that needs checking.
My **reserve and nearby jobs** leave choices if construction hours later fall.
do: **Continue** well-paid temporary works shifts while they remain available.
**Review** mortgage balance with partner each year.
**Pay extra** from future wages while shifts and school costs permit.
feel: **Uneasy** about distant crew changes, with time and local options.
S4.quote: The eight-month reserve stays for emergencies, not a paper claim that the mortgage disappeared.
fieldNote: He plans **new mortgage payments** from future wages only if well-paid shifts continue and school costs allow.
His 2039 outlook is **uneasy** despite strong assets because he cannot guarantee a smaller loan or continued site demand.

steps.text: Continue paid temporary works shifts while available
Review mortgage balance with partner annually
Pay extra mortgage from future wages if shifts and school costs permit

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable site robots around 2031 could cut walkway shifts before the mortgage is much smaller. A written crew plan and actual posted local jobs paying enough to cover the mortgage would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who signs for a walkway when a robot puts it up and a child from the next building uses it. A site plan cannot carry the responsibility for a loose guardrail. A named worker has to check the finished work.

headlineQuote: A site plan cannot carry the responsibility for a loose guardrail.
portrait: **Umar**, 43, is a mid-level site carpenter with a vocational certificate and higher pay from difficult temporary works shifts.
His pharmacy-worker partner and two schoolchildren share a **mortgage**; he has eight months of expenses saved.
He has **never used AI**, prefers paper checks and has plentiful nearby building firms to consider if shifts fall.
Rapid site robots make him **anxious** about carpentry wages, while a longer runway favours new mortgage payments over speculative training.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** may bring capable site robots around 2031 before the mortgage is much smaller.
whatWouldHelp: A **written crew plan** and posted local roles with mortgage-covering pay would give him a workable fallback.
